reason: Without hints I hesitated on full-disk encryption (it protects a physical laptop, so is it Physical?) and on whether background checks are anything more than a step in hiring. The attacker-defeats test settles both: a thief holding the laptop still has to break crypto logic (Technical), and a bad hire has to get past a process imposed on people (Administrative). It overlaps with hint 1's 'enforcer, not asset' idea but takes a different angle (the attacker's view rather than the enforcer's). Minor oddity: an outside attacker never really 'defeats' an AUP, but the three-way wording still lands it in Administrative.

My hesitations were the honesty lures: telling a client the engagement is beyond my skills (II or III?), reporting a peer selling exam questions (II or IV?), and the sales-pitch item (II or III/IV?). The hint gives a specific tie-break: honesty is Canon II only when honesty or legality is the whole point. That moves the out-of-depth disclosure to III and the exam-question report to IV, while the sales pitch (no principal yet, honesty is the point) and the unauthorised scan stay in II. Hint 0's 'owed even if nobody hired you' test already covers the III cases, but not honesty versus profession. Small residual risk: a learner could read refusing to fearmonger as 'looking after the profession' and push it to IV.

It targets a real trap: the prompt says the risk has already been 'raised', which tempts you to skip identification and start with likelihood x impact. The hint says raising isn't understanding and asks what you need to write down before you can compare. That puts asset/threat/vulnerability identification ahead of assessment and ranking. It only resolves the first pair, but that pair is genuinely prone to error here.

My main hesitation was the last two steps: is residual risk accepted when the treatment is chosen, or after the control is in place? The evidence-timing test turns the order into a chain: a register, then a ranking, then a treatment decision, then verification results, then a signed acceptance of the residual risk. Verified residual risk can't exist before the control is applied and checked, so acceptance comes last. Slight edge case: a planned residual-risk figure could in principle be written at treatment time, but 'verify it actually works' makes the verified version later.

The item I hesitated on was 'All production servers must run the approved hardened OS image' (Standard or Policy?). Applied literally, the 'replace every technology next year' test sends it to Policy: it names no specific product, so the sentence still holds after a full tech refresh (there would simply be a new approved image). That is the wrong way for an item that is most plausibly a Standard, since it mandates a specific configuration baseline. The test only clearly separates AES-256 (which names a technology) and the procedures. It also mostly rephrases hint 0's 'goal with no how vs named technology or setting' axis, so it adds little and misleads on the one ambiguous item.
